problem_statement: The paper frames currency arbitrage in the foreign exchange market as a graph-based optimization problem: find profitable exchange cycles in a currency network. It specifically models bid and ask rates to capture more realistic trading conditions and arbitrage profitability.
problem_statement_quotes: Detecting arbitrage opportunities in the foreign exchange market is computationally challenging, as the problem’s NP-completeness causes complexity to grow rapidly with the size of the currency network.

Arbitrage — the practice of profiting from price differences of an asset — is a key mechanism in the foreign exchange (FX) market, the world’s largest and most liquid financial market with over $6.6 trillion traded daily [19].
This work integrates bid and ask rates into the problem formulation for more realistic arbitrage modeling
classical_baseline: The paper treats Bellman–Ford and linear programming as the classical approaches for arbitrage detection, and also presents binary integer programming as a classical optimization formulation. These are the methods it compares against conceptually before moving to QAOA-based optimization.
classical_baseline_quotes: Traditional methods like the Bellman–Ford algorithm or linear programming, while effective for smaller networks, struggle to scale due to the exponential growth of the search space and the NP-completeness of arbitrage detection [3].
Arbitrage opportunities can be identified using classical methods such as the Bellman–Ford algorithm [23].
Alternatively, arbitrage can be formulated as a combinatorial optimization problem via binary integer programming (BIP) [21]:
classical_difficulty: The paper says the classical difficulty comes from NP-completeness, rapid growth of the search space, and poor scaling on large currency graphs. It also notes practical limitations from market frictions, transaction costs, and rapidly changing rates.
classical_difficulty_quotes: Detecting arbitrage opportunities in the foreign exchange market is computationally challenging, as the problem’s NP-completeness causes complexity to grow rapidly with the size of the currency network.

Traditional methods like the Bellman–Ford algorithm or linear programming, while effective for smaller networks, struggle to scale due to the exponential growth of the search space and the NP-completeness of arbitrage detection [3].
Moreover, its time complexity of 𝑂(|𝑉||𝐸|) becomes prohibitive on large graphs [5].
business_stakes: The paper says the financial relevance is that the method aims to recover arbitrage profit in FX trading, and that leaving profit unexploited is negligible only when the gap is under one basis point. It also ties the problem to transaction costs, bid–ask spreads, and practical feasibility on real-time or larger FX networks.
business_stakes_quotes: The difference, known as the bid–ask spread, represents transaction costs and dealer profit, influencing both arbitrage feasibility and profitability.

In currency trading terms, such a gap corresponds to leaving under one basis point of potential profit unexploited per cycle — a level negligible compared to typical transaction costs or bid–ask spreads.
Extending beyond simulation to real backends will be essential to evaluate noise resilience and establish the practical feasibility of applying quantum optimization to arbitrage.
Additionally, optimizing GCME for real-time processing could enhance its adaptability to time-sensitive optimization problems.
extraction_notes: Clear motivation in abstract and introduction; classical difficulty and business stakes are explicitly stated.
